claims.text: The initial alloy is in a metastable solid-solution-containing state.
Stepwise annealing between approximately 300 °C and 500 °C induces localized Mg segregation at defect clusters and grain boundaries.
Localized Mg-enrichment zones act as preferential nucleation sites for intermetallic compounds.
Mild thermal activation kinetically facilitates Mg segregation and chemical inhomogeneity.
Mg-containing Mg-Ti-Zn-like alloys can contain both solid-solution domains and intermetallic phases.
The spatial distribution, morphology, and size of intermetallic phases influence corrosion performance.
A fine, uniformly distributed intermetallic population can promote a protective passivating surface film and high corrosion resistance.
Fine and coherent intermetallics stabilize protective oxides responsible for high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Intermetallics can produce micro-galvanic coupling that accelerates localized dissolution of the Mg matrix.
Excessive, coalesced, or continuous intermetallic networks disrupt protective-film integrity through galvanic interactions and phase coarsening.
Annealed samples will develop distinct, finely dispersed Mg-rich clusters correlated with intermetallic nucleation.
Samples with a fine-scale intermetallic distribution will maintain or enhance corrosion resistance relative to the as-processed state.
Samples with a fine-scale intermetallic distribution will maintain or enhance high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-processed state.
Samples with continuous or coarse intermetallic networks will exhibit diminished corrosion resistance.
Samples with continuous or coarse intermetallic networks will exhibit diminished high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The relevant service-temperature regime is bounded by the thermal-stability limit of the inert treatment atmosphere.
The transition from beneficial to detrimental intermetallic distributions depends on segregation kinetics and as-yet-uncalibrated thresholds.
